# Experiments

Start with `python scripts/read_evidence.py --section brief`. It returns the initial explanation, section summaries, experiment index, saved-file paths and prediction-versus-measurement cases together. This stage plans the full experiment group: Activation search, Clusters, Inside the neuron, Where it sits, Circuit and Tests.

Use `--sections SECTION ...` to read several complete evidence sections in one call and `--ids ID ...` to read several complete cases together. Inspect the contexts and measurements needed for each hypothesis using the returned IDs and paths. The API reference below gives the input formats. Full texts, traces and measurements remain available through the reader and referenced JSON files.

## References

- [API reference](references/api-reference.md): one experiment plan, measurements and blind tests.
- [Workflow](references/workflows.md): evidence, measurement, naming and handoff.

## Work

In an existing-only run, follow the Existing-data runs section of the workflow: read CPU coactivation, reuse measurements, label the activation spectrum and semantic groups, prepare unmeasured text tests, and complete the report without new inference.

Activation spectrum and Inside the neuron use the incoming explanation's frozen response_rules. The incoming buckets contain at most three positive groups, at most three negative groups, and one No visible cue group for indistinguishable directions. Agent 1's submission has already been followed by one labeling call for the shared 500 natural-corpus points. Read the existing independent predictions through scripts/read_evidence.py --section response_predictions. scripts/label_spectrum.py returns the saved rule groups and counts; submit {} to inspect them. Keep these definitions fixed during this stage. The independent labeler sees complete observed prefixes and anchor positions without measured activations, gates, up values or previous topic labels. The host bins spectrum samples by their actual activations and colours them by predicted rule membership. Opposite-side colours are prediction disagreements and remain visible.

skill_files.text:
---
name: experiment
description: Design and measure neuron-paper contrasts, RelP graphs, routes and independent tests.
disable-model-invocation: true
metadata:
  disco-role: operating
---

# Experiments

Start with `python scripts/read_evidence.py --section brief`. It returns the initial explanation, section summaries, experiment index, saved-file paths and prediction-versus-measurement cases together. This stage plans the full experiment group: Activation search, Clusters, Inside the neuron, Where it sits, Circuit and Tests.

Use `--sections SECTION ...` to read several complete evidence sections in one call and `--ids ID ...` to read several complete cases together. Inspect the contexts and measurements needed for each hypothesis using the returned IDs and paths. The API reference below gives the input formats. Full texts, traces and measurements remain available through the reader and referenced JSON files.

## References

- [API reference](references/api-reference.md): one experiment plan, measurements and blind tests.
- [Workflow](references/workflows.md): evidence, measurement, naming and handoff.

## Work

In an existing-only run, follow the Existing-data runs section of the workflow: read CPU coactivation, reuse measurements, label the activation spectrum and semantic groups, prepare unmeasured text tests, and complete the report without new inference.

Activation spectrum and Inside the neuron use the incoming explanation's frozen response_rules. The incoming buckets contain at most three positive groups, at most three negative groups, and one No visible cue group for indistinguishable directions. Agent 1's submission has already been followed by one labeling call for the shared 500 natural-corpus points. Read the existing independent predictions through scripts/read_evidence.py --section response_predictions. scripts/label_spectrum.py returns the saved rule groups and counts; submit {} to inspect them. Keep these definitions fixed during this stage. The independent labeler sees complete observed prefixes and anchor positions without measured activations, gates, up values or previous topic labels. The host bins spectrum samples by their actual activations and colours them by predicted rule membership. Opposite-side colours are prediction disagreements and remain visible.

Keep the incoming response buckets fixed: at most three positive, at most three negative, and one No visible cue. The spectrum and scatter reuse the same independent predictions for identical inputs. Preserve counterexamples and ambiguous cases for the revision stage. Put the three most informative figures first, covering observed poles and a meaningful rival or boundary case; additional experiments remain available in the report's expandable figures. Unit labels are short noun phrases; put experimental reasoning in the section explanation or caption.

When consolidating semantic groups or defining Inside the neuron scatter clusters, use contextual meanings that describe their members. Activation sign is an observed property of each measured token. It cannot be reassigned by a semantic label. A group with both signs needs an account of the differing contexts or an explicit unresolved explanation. Repeated strong disagreements require revisiting a definition; do not preserve a directional claim by calling all disagreements exceptions. Small nonzero responses retain their sign but provide weak evidence for a semantic response. Read the measured sign counts, ranges and concrete prefixes before drawing conclusions.

For English annotations, use approximately 35–55 words for the Activation spectrum introduction, 45–70 for Activation search, approximately 30 words for Circuit, and 25–50 for other section introductions. Cluster stories and figure captions are approximately 35–65 words. Describe the pattern and strongest qualification, with detailed measurements in the evidence. These are writing targets rather than response limits.

Choose representative positive, negative and intermediate cases. Submit one measurement group with:
- Plan replacement sweeps separately for the observed positive and negative tails. Include at least one controlled sweep for each observed pole; use the remaining sweep to distinguish the strongest alternative. Mark each sweep pole as positive, negative or both. A weaker positive control is not a negative-pole experiment. For a mixed or unclear tail, test its leading explanation against matched alternatives and keep that uncertainty visible. Negative experiments normally use min scoring; positive experiments normally use max scoring. Choose a common scored span or anchor before measuring, and retain the relevant observed prefix. Do not invent an unobserved second pole. Reuse completed sweeps when continuing a run; add only an uncovered pole.
- Three illustrated RelP graphs covering the observed positive and negative neuron roots plus a distinct mechanism, boundary case or output-logit root. Select exactly three representative measured graphs for publication; if extra graphs were needed during investigation, keep their data and submit only the three selected IDs in annotations.graph_ids. Use the configured attribution node and edge counts.
  Choose readable, representative inputs that expose the proposed cue and the scored response, rather than choosing only the largest corpus extrema. State which diagnostic cue actually occurs before the anchor; a following phone number or other continuation is not yet an input cause. An indirect entity association or background case is useful as a contrast, but should not be the only positive illustration. Retain the complete observed prefix for computation and distinguish first-token or generic-context contributions from semantic cues when describing the graph.
  An output-logit illustration should target a plausible next token supported by the measured baseline predictions. Do not automatically choose the concept's name as the output token. A deliberately unlikely output target is a contrast and must be described as such.
- Search candidates and matched controls for both observed poles.
- Saved anatomy examples and a joint family comparison using the short written inputs described below.

## Published comparisons and joint traces

Each replacement figure has exactly ten measured conditions in one fixed template, including the headline comparison. For the headline, choose candidates spanning likely positive responses, likely negative responses and unrelated controls from the current evidence. A useful design is four positive candidates, four negative candidates and two unrelated controls. These are experimental expectations; retain the measured signs and failures. Use the same response anchor or span and reduction for all ten conditions. Keep weak controls and contrary results in the figure. Submit the chosen measured sweep ID as annotations.headline_figure_id. Every other published replacement figure also uses ten conditions. Do not combine conditions measured at incompatible locations just to fill rows.

For Where it sits, author eleven short diagnostic inputs: one readable showcase sentence, followed by ten matched sentences or stems that vary the relevant cue. Use the current neuron's evidence to design these texts. The complete input must show both the cue and the proposed response location. Aim for 7–29 English words and roughly 10–40 model tokens per matched input; the showcase can use up to 44 words when necessary. Retain the exact supplied texts and any meaningful trailing whitespace. These are independently written tests, not excerpts silently cut out of captured corpus inputs. Use paper.family.cases with {text, position:-1}; all positions are measured for the joint heatmap. Natural corpus experiments continue to use their complete captured prefixes.

Use the configured ten upstream and ten downstream neighbours plus the target for the joint traces, giving 21 rows when both sides are available. The host measures these units together on each of the eleven inputs. Give each displayed unit a short label of about 3–7 words supported by its measured response. Submit the complete family once; later rounds can omit family to preserve it. Change it only when a new joint test is needed.

For Circuit, measure the configured thirty downstream reader candidates and retain the measured upstream candidates. Do not replace that reader pool with a shorter list for convenience. Late-layer targets can have fewer available downstream layers. Write a summary of approximately 30 English words, explaining the measured relationship and its scope; individual units and numbers belong in the table.

Read /control/settings.json for the experiment and sampling parameters. The host selects the natural atlas, preserves original token IDs from document start through the anchor, and adds representative cases from each semantic group. Plan the configured rounds: initial tests, then strong counterexamples and matched alternatives.

Every candidate, control and replacement declares its scored token or span and reduction before measurement. Distinguish the changed cue from the response location. Use the same rule for matched conditions. Existing natural cases retain their saved anchor. There is no implicit maximum over a replacement or a full sentence.

State the changed cue, the response token/span and why that location tests the hypothesis in each prediction. A marker's token_offset is an index inside that marker: -1 selects its last token, not the token before the marker. Choose the response location from the hypothesis rather than copying an example offset. To test a response before a value is supplied, score the actual boundary before that value; the last token of an already completed value tests a different hypothesis. A trailing space, when measured, is part of the input. Preserve it explicitly. Cue-token responses and later response-slot responses are separate measurements.

Read the returned selected token, scored_positions and native trace when interpreting a contrast. A near-zero result at one token establishes only a near-zero response at that token; it does not establish that the neuron stayed inactive elsewhere. Keep failed and flat tests visible, while giving the main illustrated figures to tests that meaningfully distinguish the proposed explanations. A strong counterexample belongs among those main figures. A large bar produced only by scaling tiny residual values is not a strong effect.

The host automatically registers every new completed condition, measures target zeroing with same-layer random controls, and computes background local RelP. Same input/anchor/settings reuse their recorded measurements. These follow-ups feed What it does and the measured route data. Natural examples define the atlas; probe assignments remain identified as probes. Choose representative multi-hop display graphs separately.

Blind maximum and Blind minimum are a fixed final measurement step of this stage. The host runs the isolated writer at completion unless matching complete results already exist. You may call scripts/run_tests.py earlier to inspect them; completion reuses that result. The writer sees only the frozen initial explanation, writes the configured positive and negative candidates, and the host measures their full-input maximum and minimum before comparing them with the saved corpus extremes. Route prediction is disabled in this pipeline; leave that report slot as —.

Activation spectrum and Inside the neuron display the same 500 natural-corpus points and reuse the saved initial predictions. Their measured activation, gate and up values remain attached to those points. Read scripts/read_evidence.py --section response_predictions for errors and unresolved cases that may motivate experiments. This stage preserves the initial explanation and rules; the revision stage receives the feedback.

Complete with a result summary and annotations using the full JSON example in the API reference. Each annotations.routes value is an object with name and description; each annotations.units value is a label string; section prose uses an object with summary. Use measured route and unit IDs from the results. Completion returns the experimental report with the incoming claim unchanged. Submit after the measurements, spectrum labels and independent tests; this task does not revise the claim.

## Semantic Clusters and raw routes

A route is a numerical contribution pattern, not a semantic category. Keep its measured membership intact in Raw factorization. After the configured measurement rounds and scripts/run_tests.py have returned, read scripts/read_evidence.py --section routes. This gives the complete current natural-training member index. Use --section routes --ids GRAPH_ID ... to read complete observed prefixes, native traces, selected anchors and upstream vectors. The index previews are navigation aids, not sufficient evidence for deciding a member's meaning. Read every member's complete context before assigning it. Read the latest index again if you add experiments after it.

Organize those measured members into reader-facing semantic clusters. Several routes may contribute to one cluster; one route may contain members belonging to different clusters. Use the text, scored position, activation and upstream contributions together. An existing spectrum label is a hint, not a compulsory assignment. Similar text does not prove the same mechanism; similar contributions do not prove the same topic.

Give every member one display cluster, without dropping weak activations, mismatches or counterexamples. Use mixed or unresolved clusters when no supported common account exists. Explain when a numerical route crosses semantic categories. If splitting out a member limits a proposed explanation, retain that limitation explicitly in the affected story; do not use regrouping to make contrary evidence disappear.

For each cluster, state its membership criterion, the shared observations or contribution patterns, and the important exceptions or uncertainty. A name inferred from a few strong examples must not silently describe all remaining members. The tools derive response summaries from the measured members. Explain positive and negative conditions from those measurements; leave unresolved causes explicit.

Choose up to three example_graph_ids from the cluster's actual graph_ids. Show a typical case and, whenever one is informative, a boundary case or counterexample. Do not merely choose the first or highest-activation members. The complete member list remains in the structured report.

Return annotations.clusters as an array of {id, name, story, graph_ids, example_graph_ids}. Use graph_id values from the routes evidence, not saved case IDs or route IDs. The fixed tools derive member_routes, graph counts, attribution-mass shares, upstream summaries and original example values. Do not supply those numbers. Raw routes retain their own annotations.routes name/description mapping.

## Writing

Write a short title in the form “[concept] neuron”, with an optional phrase describing its response. Begin the explanation directly with what this neuron responds to or changes. Refer to the measured unit as “this neuron”; keep its layer and index in the identification fields.

Use ordinary descriptions of the positive and negative responses. Describe sparsity in the activation-distribution discussion, rather than calling the neuron a “sparse feature”. Keep qualifications in sentences instead of stacking them in a long title.

Describe the observations and conclusions directly for the reader.

skill_files.name: references/api-reference.md
skill_files.text:
# Experiments API

Read `/control/settings.json` for the experiment and sampling parameters. Submit hypotheses, texts, source cases and explicit scoring locations.

## Read evidence

```bash
mkdir -p /workspace/reads
python scripts/read_evidence.py --section brief > /workspace/reads/brief.json
python scripts/read_evidence.py --sections distribution peak_census output_effects > /workspace/reads/statistics.json
python scripts/read_evidence.py --section contexts --group top_tokens --offset 0 --limit 4 > /workspace/reads/top_tokens.json
```

The brief combines interpretation, section summaries, experiment_index (including paths and JSON file names), figure and graph descriptions, cluster definitions and prediction feedback. Its prediction cases retain complete observed prefixes and anchors, ordered with strong directional errors first. Use --limit for the number of feedback cases. Use --sections to read several complete evidence sections in one call; use --ids ID ... to fetch several complete contexts or route members together. Choose further reads from the returned IDs and paths. Complete requested records remain available.

Use /workspace/reads for your own exports. /workspace/evidence also contains host-generated input.json and manifest.json; manifest.json.cases is a count, whereas a contexts response has a cases list. Read the context files you exported rather than treating every JSON file in the internal evidence directory as a context page.

Other sections: distribution, token_selectivity, peak_census, gate_value, output_effects, measurements and routes. Request contexts by saved IDs when needed. Use --section measurements to list compact experiment overviews and --section measurements --ids EXPERIMENT_ID to inspect one experiment's status, values, directory and JSON file names. The complete artifacts remain in that directory.

saved_analysis is generated only when existing_only is true. An inference run does not create it. In measured results, anatomy_cases is a count, not a list; follow-up conditions is a count, whereas replacement-sweep conditions is a list. Read the named values directly, and use the referenced raw files for traces and detailed tables.

## Read raw routes and organize semantic Clusters

Run the configured independent tests before this read so the index includes the final natural-atlas members. This read performs no experiments.

```bash
printf '%s\n' '{}' | python scripts/run_tests.py
python scripts/read_evidence.py --section routes > /workspace/reads/routes.json
python scripts/read_evidence.py --section routes --group p1
python scripts/read_evidence.py --section routes --ids MEASURED_GRAPH_ID
```

For run_tests.py, supply an empty JSON object through stdin or --input FILE (see the Independent tests section). Replace p1 and MEASURED_GRAPH_ID with IDs returned by this run.

The index contains every natural training route member, its graph_id, raw route_id, selected token/position/product, existing semantic_group when available, upstream contributors and NMF route weights. context_preview is only a navigation preview. --ids returns complete observed text and native trace; no full-prefix measurement changes. --group filters the member index by a raw route ID. semantic_clusters contains the previous submitted definitions in a revision stage.

Semantic grouping uses graph_id, not the corpus case_id. Account for all index members exactly once in the display grouping. Raw routes are retained independently. Merge routes or split their members when the evidence supports it; retain mixed, unresolved and contrary cases. Names and stories must describe the actual scope and exceptions. Choose up to three examples, including an informative counterexample when present.

## Submit a group

```json
{
  "analysis": "The hypothesis, competing explanation and predicted difference.",
  "round": 1,
  "sweeps": [{
    "title": "A controlled replacement test",
    "pole": "positive",
    "prediction": "How changing the cue should change the specified response.",
    "template": "<fixed prefix> {slot}<single-token response marker><fixed suffix>",
    "replacements": [
      "<candidate 1>", "<candidate 2>", "<candidate 3>", "<candidate 4>",
      "<opposite-pole candidate 1>", "<opposite-pole candidate 2>",
      "<opposite-pole candidate 3>", "<opposite-pole candidate 4>",
      "<unrelated control 1>", "<unrelated control 2>"
    ],
    "score": {
      "location": "marker",
      "text": "<single-token response marker>",
      "occurrence": 0,
      "token_offset": 0,
      "reduction": "single"
    }
  }],
  "graphs": [{
    "title": "A representative saved context",
    "prediction": "Which observed response this graph explains.",
    "case_id": "<ID from evidence>",
    "root": {"kind":"neuron_product"}
  }],
  "paper": {
    "search": [{
      "id": "hypothesis-a",
      "name": "<hypothesis>",
      "pole": "positive",
      "rival": "<alternative>",
      "score": {"location":"marker","text":"<single-token response marker>","token_offset":0,"reduction":"single"},
      "candidates": [{"text":"<candidate input>"}],
      "controls": [{"text":"<matched control input>"}]
    }],
    "atlas": {"cases":["<optional additional saved ID>"]},
    "family": {"cases":[
      {"text":"<short authored showcase>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 1>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 2>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 3>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 4>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 5>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 6>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 7>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 8>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 9>","position":-1},
      {"text":"<matched written input 10>","position":-1}
    ]},
    "anatomy": {"sentence":{"case_id":"<saved ID>"}}
  }
}
```

These strings illustrate the API. Replace them with choices from the target evidence. Send the JSON to `python scripts/run_experiments.py`.

Routes per pole, neighbour counts, attribution node and edge counts, controls and prefix policy are applied by the tools from settings.json. Specify hypotheses, texts and scored locations in the request.

## Scoring

Declare the location and reduction before measuring candidates. Candidates and matched controls use the same rule. A candidate may carry its own explicit score when its frame requires a different marker.

For marker scoring, occurrence is the zero-based occurrence of the literal marker text. token_offset indexes the tokens overlapping that marker: 0 is its first token and -1 is its last token. It does not move to the token before the marker. With no token_offset, the declared reduction applies to all tokens overlapping the marker. The single-token markers below are format examples, not a recommendation to score the beginning or end of every phrase. Choose the actual token from the scientific hypothesis and name it in prediction.

For an upcoming-value hypothesis, the response is before the value begins, not at the last digit or word after the value has already been supplied. One option is to end each matched written input at the intended boundary and use {"location":"token_position","position":-1,"reduction":"single"}; then -1 means the last token of that entire input. Preserve any intended trailing whitespace. The returned selected.token and selected.position identify the measured token. Compare a cue-span score separately when needed; do not substitute a whole-input maximum for a declared response-slot measurement.

```json
[
  {
    "location": "marker",
    "text": "<single-token response marker>",
    "occurrence": 0,
    "token_offset": 0,
    "reduction": "single"
  },
  {
    "location": "token_position",
    "position": 12,
    "reduction": "single"
  },
  {
    "location": "replacement_span",
    "reduction": "max"
  },
  {
    "location": "after_replacement",
    "reduction": "min"
  },
  {
    "location": "input",
    "reduction": "max"
  }
]
```

There is no implicit replacement-span or whole-input maximum. If the cue and a later response slot are both of interest, submit two explicitly named measurements. Natural saved cases keep their original anchor coordinate. The records retain scored_positions and the actual selected token.

## Full original prefixes

A saved case resolves to its original token IDs from document position0 through its anchor, inclusive. The host neither retokenizes it nor drops earlier tokens. The next saved token is recorded as a prediction target. Atlas, family, illustrated saved-case graphs and follow-up measurements share this policy.

Written inputs use the configured maximum token length, without silent truncation. A written graph has `text` and an explicit root `position` or `marker`; a saved graph uses `case_id` and the host's original anchor. Output-logit roots additionally name `token_text`.

## Automatic follow-ups

Every group has one model worker. The host registers the configured positive/negative natural extreme references and each completed sweep, search, atlas or selected-graph condition, then automatically measures:

- Native gate, value and product at the full-prefix anchor.
- Target-neuron zeroing and configured same-layer random-neuron controls.
- Next-token distribution changes and local RelP upstream/downstream vectors.

Identical inputs/anchors/settings reuse their saved registry measurements. The response identifies completed and failed conditions.

The registry, raw logits, contribution vectors and source references are stored under the group's followups directory. New probes receive route assignments from factors fitted on natural training cases. Circuit continues to aggregate the natural atlas. Probe results remain separately identifiable.

Named semantic groups also contribute representative saved anchors, covering each observed sign where available. The host adds pending group representatives before stage two completes. Agent-selected illustrated graphs retain the full multi-hop RelP drawing; other conditions receive background contribution vectors.

## Spectrum and labels

The incoming response_rules define the spectrum's response groups: at most three positive, at most three negative, and one No visible cue group for cases with no distinguishable direction. The host has already frozen these definitions and obtained independent text-only assignments. Use the evidence reader's response_predictions section to inspect errors and ambiguous cases.

To read the current group definitions and counts:

```json
{}
```

```bash
python scripts/label_spectrum.py --input /workspace/request.json
```

The tool returns groups, n_requested, explanation_version, reused, llm_requests and new_model_forwards. It reuses the incoming predictions. Do not submit a new topic taxonomy during this stage. Both views keep the same 500 natural-corpus points and saved initial predictions.

Every spectrum point keeps its observed activation and bin. Colour follows the predicted response group: positive, negative or uncertain. Opposite-sign members are retained as counterexamples. The scatter and spectrum share one prediction for an identical observed prefix and anchor. Full API records are saved by the tools.

## Independent tests

Call `scripts/run_tests.py` once. The writer receives the frozen initial explanation. Candidate count and text length come from settings.json. Its declared metric is the maximum or minimum over the written input. These measured candidates automatically receive the same follow-up calculations.

Route prediction is disabled in this pipeline. Its report slot stays —.

## Complete

The complete example below specifies the input shape. Replace its prose and IDs with measured findings and IDs from this run. It is not an interpretation example. Empty optional mappings may remain {}.

```json
{
  "summary": "Summarize the measured findings and remaining alternatives.",
  "annotations": {
    "headline_figure_id": "MEASURED_SWEEP_ID",
    "graph_ids": ["MEASURED_DISPLAY_GRAPH_ID_A", "MEASURED_DISPLAY_GRAPH_ID_B", "MEASURED_DISPLAY_GRAPH_ID_C"],
    "routes": {
      "MEASURED_ROUTE_ID": {
        "name": "Name supported by the measured route examples",
        "description": "Explain the examples and upstream contributions for this measured route."
      }
    },
    "clusters": [
      {
        "id": "c1",
        "name": "Evidence-supported semantic cluster",
        "story": "Membership criterion, observed shared contribution pattern, and exceptions or unresolved evidence.",
        "graph_ids": ["MEASURED_GRAPH_ID_A", "MEASURED_GRAPH_ID_B"],
        "example_graph_ids": ["MEASURED_GRAPH_ID_A", "MEASURED_GRAPH_ID_B"]
      }
    ],
    "units": {
      "L0_N0": "Description supported by the measured unit evidence"
    },
    "sections": {
      "spectrum": {
        "summary": "Explain semantic group counts and activation ranges as counts of the selected samples."
      },
      "search": {
        "summary": "Explain the measured candidates and matched controls at their declared score positions."
      },
      "clusters": {
        "summary": "Explain the measured route groups and their distinctions."
      },
      "anatomy": {
        "summary": "Explain the measured gate/value/product patterns.",
        "strip_caption": "Describe the selected saved trace."
      },
      "ablation": {
        "summary": "Explain direct output weights and measured neuron-zeroing effects."
      },
      "family": {
        "summary": "Explain the joint measured traces of this neuron and its neighbours."
      },
      "circuit": {
        "summary": "Explain the measured upstream and downstream contributions."
      },
      "tests": {
        "summary": "Explain the measured independent blind tests and their outcomes."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Save the object to /workspace/completion.json and call:

```bash
python scripts/complete_experiments.py --input /workspace/completion.json
```

Fields:

- summary: the experiment findings as a string.
- annotations.headline_figure_id: a measured replacement sweep ID with ten conditions in one frame, covering likely positive, likely negative and unrelated inputs. The renderer uses its complete measured comparison.
- annotations.graph_ids: exactly three measured multi-hop display graph IDs in the desired order. Use IDs returned by graphs, not the local route-atlas graph_ids used in semantic clusters. Other measured graphs remain in saved artifacts.
- paper.family.cases: eleven explicit written inputs, one showcase plus ten matched variations. Each has text and position. The host measures every token for joint traces. Omit family in later rounds to reuse the completed family. Use the configured neighbours; unit labels are provided at completion.
- annotations.routes: keyed by actual measured route ID, such as a route returned in measured_sections.routes. Each value is an object with name and description. A route value is not a plain string.
- annotations.clusters: a complete array of semantic cluster definitions in the shape above. Each graph_id comes from the latest routes index. The measured membership may cross raw route boundaries. Counts, shares, key units and example activations are derived by the host. Submitted members are never removed from raw routes; any unassigned measured members remain visible as unassigned contexts.
- annotations.units: keyed by a measured Lx_Ny identifier. Each value is a label string, not a name/description object. L0_N0 above only illustrates the key syntax; replace it with a measured unit or leave units empty.
- annotations.sections: keyed by the section names shown above. Use an object with summary. Anatomy may also contain strip_caption. Plain strings are supported for section prose, but the complete example uses summary objects consistently.
- Put output effects and zeroing findings in ablation (What it does); upstream/downstream contributions belong to circuit.
- This call connects saved numerical data to the report, adds the configured pending follow-ups and blind tests if needed, labels newly measured points, and renders HTML. A previous successful blind test is reused. Repeated completion calls can regenerate HTML, so submit the finished annotations rather than probing the format by rendering trial pages.
- The host preserves the incoming claim for stage three. This stage's summary and annotations do not replace the final claim revision.


Existing-only runs retain their existing-only workflow: they do not submit numerical experiments or automatic GPU follow-ups.

## Frozen-explanation response predictions

Use `python scripts/read_evidence.py --section response_predictions --limit 4` for prediction-versus-measurement feedback. The response includes the frozen claim and rules, separate feedback/seen/experiment counts, and full-prefix cases ordered with strong directional errors first. Use `--ids`, `--group`, `--offset` and `--limit` to inspect cases. Keep the initial claim and response_rules fixed in this stage; design experiments that clarify their errors and uncertain conditions.

skill_files.text:
# Experiment workflow

Read the incoming explanation, saved evidence and /control/settings.json.

1. Identify competing accounts for the observed positive and negative responses. Read complete observed prefixes. Following text is a prediction target.
2. Define the complete semantic-group catalog from those contexts and submit it together using the full label_spectrum JSON example. A fresh call processes all unique saved report positions; one group is not a small trial. See the API reference for exact-match reuse and resume_from semantics.
3. Use the configured search rounds. In the first round, submit controlled hypotheses with explicit scored locations. Read the resulting measurements. In the next round, choose strong counterexamples and matched alternatives that distinguish the surviving accounts.
4. Reuse prior completed conditions. The host registers new conditions and runs their full-prefix ablations and background RelP automatically.
5. Choose positive and negative illustrated graphs from the evidence; include an output-logit root where useful. These receive the configured multi-hop graph calculation.
6. Run scripts/run_tests.py before organizing Clusters; matching completed tests are reused. This also finishes the pending semantic-group representatives through the existing measurement tools. Read the latest natural-atlas routes with scripts/read_evidence.py --section routes, then read all member contexts by graph ID. Keep raw routes separate from semantic clusters; merge or split their members only as supported by text and contribution evidence. Preserve contrary and unresolved members and describe the limitations they expose. Select representative and informative exception examples. If more experiments are added, read the latest membership again before submission.
7. Complete the experiment handoff with measured summaries and captions, using the complete_experiments JSON example: route values are name/description objects, clusters is an array with explicit graph_ids and example_graph_ids, unit values are strings, and section prose uses summary objects. The host generates the HTML. Stage three performs the final revision.

Each plan states the changed cue, fixed context, scored token/span, predicted direction and alternative explanation. Keep the same scoring rule for candidates and matched controls. A word response and a later prediction slot are distinct measurements.

Use the sampling and measurement parameters supplied in settings.json. Base hypotheses on the supplied target evidence.

## Existing-only runs

When existing_only is true, read saved coactivation and prior measurements, label semantic groups and prepare unmeasured text proposals through scripts/prepare_tests.py. No model inference or automatic GPU follow-up is available. Unmeasured results remain —. Semantic associations do not establish causal edges.

## Long tools

Tool scripts wait for the host operation to finish, then return its saved result. GPU allocation and waiting are handled by the host. A failed result stays in the records; do not repeat it merely to obtain a passing result.

## Command-line input

Every script supports --help. Read-evidence accepts --section, --group, --ids, --offset and --limit, or a JSON object through stdin. Other scripts accept JSON through redirected stdin or --input FILE. Unsupported flags and invalid JSON exit immediately with a usage error. Tools wait for the completed operation; no progress-polling loop is needed.
